papers.title: Unified Hallucination Fuzzing for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What two components make up the unified hallucination evaluation framework for multimodal LLMs, and what problem does each solve?
qa_pairs.answer: The first is UniHall, a fine-grained dataset grounded in a unified taxonomy spanning Object, Instruction, and Knowledge dimensions, which addresses the narrow taxonomical coverage of existing static benchmarks. The second is Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing (SAMF), which uses evolutionary mutation strategies to explore the boundaries of model hallucinations and thereby addresses benchmark saturation, where static benchmarks stop discriminating as models improve. Because fuzzing produces dynamic rather than fixed inputs, SAMF also incorporates a structured metric suite driven by an ensemble of multi-modal oracles so the generated cases can still be assessed reliably.

qa_pairs.question: How is the SAMF fuzzing pipeline organised, and what does a fuzzing policy specify?
qa_pairs.answer: The pipeline has three core components: an Orchestrator, a Fuzzer controlled by multiple Agents, and a unified evaluation loop. Given a seed image-question pair with ground truth and risk annotations, the Orchestrator first extracts structural attributes such as the question type (for example VQA or Yes/No) and the hallucination subcategory (object-, instruction-, or knowledge-level), and these determine the admissible mutation space. It then activates a corresponding Agent, which specifies a policy defining which textual and visual mutation operators to apply, how those operators are combined, and the fuzzing level controlling perturbation difficulty.

qa_pairs.question: How do the heuristic and reinforcement-learning variants of SAMF differ?
qa_pairs.answer: They instantiate the same general workflow and share the same policy selection mechanism, differing only in how fuzzing policies are explored and updated. The heuristic search refines policies through greedy local improvements, whereas the reinforcement-learning variant explores multiple candidate policies using feedback-driven adaptation. Keeping everything else fixed is what makes the two comparable as search strategies over the same policy space.

qa_pairs.question: What did fuzzing reveal about state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs that conventional static evaluation did not?
qa_pairs.answer: State-of-the-art MLLMs showed significant performance degradation under fuzzing compared with conventional settings, exposing a dissociation between reasoning capabilities and factual grounding: a model can reason well and still fail to stay grounded once inputs are perturbed. The authors additionally identify a helpfulness-hallucination trade-off, in which reinforcement learning alignment inadvertently exacerbates sycophancy on instruction-following tasks, so alignment intended to make models more helpful can make hallucination worse.

qa_pairs.question: What is the fourth dimension of the UniHall taxonomy, and how many text-only LLMs were fuzzed with SAMF?
qa_pairs.answer: Both halves of this question rest on false premises. The UniHall taxonomy has three dimensions, not four: Object, Instruction, and Knowledge. And no text-only LLMs were evaluated, because the framework is specifically multimodal: seed instances are image-question pairs, the mutation operators are textual and visual, and the evaluation targets multimodal large language models.

papers.title: DocAtlas: Long-Document Understanding as Mutable-State Interaction
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What does DocAtlas mean by treating long-document understanding as a mutable-state information-seeking process?
qa_pairs.answer: In a static retrieval system, pages are embedded into a fixed index and a top-k subset is selected before generation, so the retrieval state never changes during an episode. DocAtlas instead instantiates a mutable document harness: an external environment that determines what document information is searched, read, stored, reviewed, and shown to the model at each step. The harness exposes search, reading, note-taking, and review tools and maintains a hierarchical tree and a note store, updating both as the agent records evidence, so the state seen by later tool calls depends on earlier interactions.

qa_pairs.question: What results does DocAtlas report on MMLongBench-Doc, and what makes the compact-model result notable?
qa_pairs.answer: With GPT-5.4 as the backbone, DocAtlas reaches 71.4% on MMLongBench-Doc, exceeding the human-expert reference of 65.8%. Separately, a Qwen3.5-4B vision-language model trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning inside the DocAtlas environment reaches 63.7%, compared with a 54.4% direct-input baseline. The compact-model gain is the stronger claim, since it shows the harness design itself improves small document agents by a large margin rather than the result being carried by a very large proprietary backbone.

qa_pairs.question: Why does simply feeding an entire long document into a vision-language model fail?
qa_pairs.answer: Two separate reasons. First, long documents such as financial reports, legal contracts and government filings can run to hundreds of pages and quickly exceed the practical limits of current vision-language models. Second, even when the input does fit within the context window, performance often drops because irrelevant content competes for attention. Static retrieval only partly helps: it selects a fixed subset of pages but cannot refine its search as evidence accumulates.

qa_pairs.question: How does the DocAtlas paper distinguish the terms model, policy, and agent?
qa_pairs.answer: Model, or backbone, refers to the underlying vision-language model weights; policy refers to the mapping from interaction history to the next action; and agent refers to the policy running inside the DocAtlas tool environment. The same VLM is therefore described as a model when discussing architecture or size, as a policy when discussing reinforcement learning or action choices, and as an agent when it interacts with tools and the environment.

qa_pairs.question: How many epochs was GPT-5.4 fine-tuned for inside the DocAtlas environment to reach 71.4%?
qa_pairs.answer: GPT-5.4 was not fine-tuned at all, so there is no epoch count. The paper distinguishes two uses of the same harness: inference-time use with large VLMs, which is how the 71.4% GPT-5.4 result was obtained, and end-to-end reinforcement learning for compact VLM agents, which is how the Qwen3.5-4B model was trained to 63.7%. Only the compact model is trained in the environment.

papers.title: WuYuEval: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Large Language Models in Solid Waste Management
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: How is the WuYuEval benchmark for solid waste management structured?
qa_pairs.answer: WuYuEval evaluates across three levels: foundational knowledge, domain reasoning, and expert decision-making. After quality auditing it contains a Foundation Module of 4,590 closed-ended multiple-choice questions spanning six task types and eight domain categories, and an Expert Module of 247 scenario-based open-ended questions involving multi-objective optimization, constraint trade-offs, and system design. The two modules test different things: recall and calculation on one side, professional judgment under engineering, environmental and policy constraints on the other.

qa_pairs.question: How are the open-ended expert tasks in WuYuEval scored?
qa_pairs.answer: Because scenario-based answers have no single correct string, the authors combine two mechanisms: anchor-calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring, where the judge is calibrated against anchor responses rather than left to score freely, and Elo-based pairwise comparison, which ranks models by head-to-head preference. Using both gives an absolute calibrated score and a relative ranking, which is more robust than either alone for open-ended engineering answers.

qa_pairs.question: What did WuYuEval find when it evaluated 33 large language models, and where was performance weakest?
qa_pairs.answer: Performance varied widely across the 33 models. The leading model reached 94.64% accuracy on the Foundation Module, but average accuracy still fell sharply with difficulty, from 84.14% on easy questions to 42.50% on hard ones. Weakness concentrated in calculation, experimental design, urban planning, and the open-ended expert tasks, that is, precisely the categories that require applying knowledge under constraints rather than recalling it.

qa_pairs.question: What does WuYuEval conclude about whether reasoning-oriented Thinking modes help on solid waste management tasks?
qa_pairs.answer: Thinking modes improved most matched model pairs after auditing, but the gains depend on baseline capability and are not uniformly positive, so enabling deliberation is not reliably beneficial. The authors interpret this as visible deliberation helping only when it stays anchored to units, assumptions, and engineering constraints; otherwise the reasoning may drift away from decisive answer boundaries. This motivates their call for domain foundation models with professional reasoning chains and explicit constraint control.

qa_pairs.question: How many multiple-choice questions does WuYuEval's Expert Module contain, and what is its reported inter-annotator agreement?
qa_pairs.answer: The Expert Module contains no multiple-choice questions at all: it holds 247 scenario-based open-ended questions covering multi-objective optimization, constraint trade-offs, and system design. The multiple-choice items belong to the Foundation Module, which has 4,590 of them across six task types and eight domain categories. The paper also does not report an inter-annotator agreement statistic; its quality process is described as expert review and filtering together with multi-model cross-evaluation.

papers.title: Search-G1: Grounded Search Agents via Representation-Based Intrinsic Rewards
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What are the two intervention-calibrated readouts in Search-G1, and what does each measure?
qa_pairs.answer: The prompt-state readout predicts closed-book sufficiency, that is, whether the policy could answer without retrieving; its complement defines policy-relative retrieval necessity. The answer-commit readout estimates evidence reliance by measuring answer-stage sensitivity to evidence deletion, so an answer that changes when the retrieved evidence is removed counts as evidence-grounded. Both are described as policy-relative because they are defined against what this particular policy knows rather than against an absolute standard.

qa_pairs.question: Why does Search-G1 argue that existing external and internal reward signals are inadequate for grounded search agents?
qa_pairs.answer: External rewards fail in two different ways. Sparse outcome rewards scale readily but cannot distinguish grounded retrieval from redundant search, since both can produce a correct final answer. Richer signals from process annotations or LLM judges do capture the difference, but require costly annotation or extra inference during training. Internal rewards based on policy-side signals such as entropy, likelihood or information gain are graded and cheap to evaluate, but they mainly reflect model confidence rather than evidence grounding, which is the property that actually matters here.

qa_pairs.question: How does Search-G1 combine its two readouts into a reward, and what behaviours does that reward encourage?
qa_pairs.answer: The readouts jointly assign additional credit to correct searched trajectories when retrieval is estimated to be necessary and the answer is evidence-sensitive. They favour correct direct answers when closed-book knowledge already suffices, and they penalise repeated search. The effect is to reward retrieval only where it does real work, rather than rewarding retrieval as such.

qa_pairs.question: Why does Search-G1 periodically refit its readouts during training, and what does calibration buy at policy-optimization time?
qa_pairs.answer: Reinforcement learning changes the policy's internal representations, so readouts fitted on an early checkpoint would gradually stop measuring what they were built to measure. Search-G1 therefore refits both readouts on trajectories from the latest checkpoint, letting the reward co-evolve with the policy. Once calibrated, reward scoring requires neither process annotations nor LLM-as-judge inference during policy optimization, which is what keeps the method cheap relative to richer external signals.

qa_pairs.question: Which human annotators labelled the retrieval-necessity judgments that Search-G1 trains its reward on?
qa_pairs.answer: None, and avoiding exactly that cost is the point of the method. Search-G1's readouts are calibrated through interventions on the policy's own representations rather than from human process annotations, and after calibration the reward requires neither process annotations nor LLM-as-judge inference during policy optimization. The paper positions this against richer external reward signals, which do need costly annotation or inference at training time.

papers.title: Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What premise about interpretability does 'Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models' challenge, and what did its scaling experiments find?
qa_pairs.answer: The premise is that interpretability is a tax on capability: that models must be trained as opaque systems and explained after the fact by methods whose reliability is hard to establish. Instead the authors make interpretability a constraint of the training pipeline, optimized alongside the language modeling objective. Across three orders of magnitude of compute, on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, interpretability scaled with capability rather than against it, and model representations became more disentangled and more aligned with human-understandable concepts as scale increased.

qa_pairs.question: What is Steerling-8B, and what can it attribute its outputs to?
qa_pairs.answer: Steerling-8B is the instantiation of the training-time recipe: a diffusion language model with a causal attention mask. For any group of generated tokens it attributes the output to three things: the relevant input tokens, human-understandable concepts, and the training data responsible. It remains competitive with open peer models trained on substantially 2 to 16 times more compute, which is what makes the interpretability constraint look like something other than a capability sacrifice.

qa_pairs.question: What is closed-loop intervention in Steerling-8B, and why does it not require retraining?
qa_pairs.answer: Closed-loop intervention is a three-step workflow: diagnose an output through its concept or feature attribution, retrieve similar training data to understand where the behaviour came from, and then correct the behaviour through concept steering. Because the concepts are explicit modules the model was trained with rather than post-hoc reconstructions, steering them changes behaviour directly at inference, so no retraining step is needed to close the loop.

qa_pairs.question: What was the purpose of Steerling-8B's mid-training stage?
qa_pairs.answer: Mid-training is a short 150B-token run initialized from the final pretraining checkpoint, with two aims. First, to address four weaknesses identified during pretraining: aggressive masking, thin math and code coverage, an unstable independence loss, and no exposure to steering during training. Second, to tighten the model for downstream use by reducing its reliance on teacher forcing and increasing its reliance on the concept heads.

qa_pairs.question: Which sparse autoencoder was trained on Steerling-8B after pretraining to extract its interpretable concepts?
qa_pairs.answer: None was, and the premise inverts the paper's central argument. Steerling-8B does not have its concepts recovered afterwards by a post-hoc method such as a sparse autoencoder; interpretability is built in as a training constraint optimized alongside the language modeling objective, with a concept module in the architecture and a concept library constructed by the Atlas documents-to-concepts pipeline. The paper explicitly argues that post-hoc methods fail to satisfy its interpretability requirements, which is why the recipe moves them into training.

papers.title: Embedding Initialization for Unseen Low-resource Languages in Multilingual NMT: A Case Study on Limbum-English Translation
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What practical problem arises when fine-tuning NLLB-200 for a language it does not support, and what initialization strategy does this paper propose?
qa_pairs.answer: NLLB-200 prepends a language token to each source sentence, and each token has a learned embedding encoding language identity, but an unseen language has no such token. The standard workaround is to repurpose the token of a related language as a proxy, yet no principled method exists for choosing which one. The proposed strategy initializes the new language's embedding as the average of embeddings from multiple typologically related languages already in the model: select k proxies from the same family, set e_L to their mean, then add the token to the tokenizer and expand the embedding matrix by one row.

qa_pairs.question: What chrF2++ scores did the four Limbum-to-English systems achieve, and what do they show?
qa_pairs.answer: NLLB-200 zero-shot scored 12.5, a Transformer trained from scratch 14.5, NLLB-200 fine-tuned with a Swahili proxy token 47.3, and NLLB-200 with the averaged embedding initialization 46.7. The averaged initialization is therefore comparable to the best single-language proxy while removing the need to guess which proxy to use. Both NLLB-200 variants beat the from-scratch baseline by over 32 chrF2++ points, which the authors read as evidence that multilingual transfer, not architecture, dominates in extremely low-resource Bantu translation.

qa_pairs.question: Which proxy languages were chosen for the Limbum embedding initialization, and on what grounds?
qa_pairs.answer: Three Bantu languages were used. Swahili (swh_Latn, zone E.70) was chosen as the highest-resource Bantu language in NLLB. Luganda (lug_Latn, zone J.10) was chosen for being agglutinative with strong NLLB representation. Lingala (lin_Latn, zone C.30) was chosen for its proximity to the Grassfields zone that Limbum belongs to. The method rests on one assumption: that related languages occupy a coherent region of the pretrained embedding space.

qa_pairs.question: How was the Limbum-English parallel corpus built, and what failure did every system share?
qa_pairs.answer: The corpus of 8,837 sentence pairs was compiled from two bilingual resources: the Limbum New Testament published by the Bible Society of Cameroon, provided as a verse-by-verse aligned PDF, and the Limbum Dictionary by Francis Ndi Wepngong. Regardless of approach, every system failed to preserve tonal diacritics, which the authors flag as an open challenge. That failure is notable because NLLB-200's 256,000-token SentencePiece vocabulary does include the Unicode combining characters used in tonal orthographies.

qa_pairs.question: How many of the roughly 2,000 sub-Saharan African languages did the averaged-embedding method get evaluated on in this study?
qa_pairs.answer: Only one. Although the paper motivates the work by noting that over 2,000 languages are spoken in sub-Saharan Africa while NLLB-200 covers fewer than 3% of the world's roughly 7,000 living languages, the study itself is a single case study on Limbum-to-English translation. Generalisation across many languages is not part of what is reported.

papers.title: SurveyReview: A Reviewer-Aligned Benchmark for Survey Evaluators
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What gap does SurveyReview address, and how large is the dataset it introduces?
qa_pairs.answer: Large language models have turned survey writing from a months-long manual effort into an automated pipeline, which moves the bottleneck to evaluation. Existing automatic evaluators largely rely on off-the-shelf LLM-as-a-judge methods with no systematic alignment to human reviewers, and no framework existed for quantifying that alignment. SurveyReview responds with 675 annotated survey papers paired with 1,630 review reports, plus standardized train/test splits and an evaluation protocol.

qa_pairs.question: How does SurveyReview convert authentic peer review into supervision, and along which dimensions?
qa_pairs.answer: Free-form reviewer comments are restructured into four-dimensional scores paired with supporting rationales. The four dimensions are Readability, Criticalness, Comprehensiveness, and Structure. Formally, the task is a multi-dimensional scoring problem in which an evaluation of paper P is a set of triples E = {(d_i, s_i, r_i)}, each holding a quality dimension, a numeric score, and a rationale, so an evaluator must justify a score rather than only emit one.

qa_pairs.question: What is SurveyAlign, and how much does it improve alignment with human reviewers?
qa_pairs.answer: SurveyAlign is the paper's baseline evaluator, built by fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with LoRA on the annotated data and augmenting it with external knowledge for the knowledge-intensive dimensions. On the test set it substantially outperforms prompt-based judging with GPT-5.2, reducing average mean squared error from 2.28 to 1.38 and mean absolute error from 1.15 to 0.69 across all four dimensions. The comparison is the paper's evidence that alignment comes from training on reviewer data rather than from a stronger backbone.

qa_pairs.question: Why does SurveyReview measure alignment with human reviewers rather than absolute evaluation quality?
qa_pairs.answer: Because the ground truth it can obtain is expert judgment itself. Collecting high-quality annotations from domain experts at scale is prohibitively expensive, so the benchmark leverages existing peer-review reports as the expert signal, treating the reviewer's four-dimensional score and rationale as E*. Evaluator quality is then measured as mean squared error and mean absolute error between an automatic evaluator's scores and those reviewer scores, per dimension.

qa_pairs.question: How many survey papers did SurveyAlign itself generate for the benchmark, and what was their acceptance rate?
qa_pairs.answer: The question mixes up the two sides of the pipeline. SurveyAlign is an evaluator, not a generator: it scores surveys along the four reviewer-aligned dimensions and produces no surveys of its own, so it has no acceptance rate. The 675 surveys in the benchmark were collected and annotated with their 1,630 existing review reports rather than generated, and survey generation systems such as AutoSurvey, SurveyGen and SurveyX are discussed as related work rather than used to build the dataset.

papers.title: Evaluating Dedicated Monolingual and Joint Multilingual Causal Models for Dravidian Languages
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What five models were trained for the Dravidian language comparison, and how did their tokenizers differ?
qa_pairs.answer: Five GPT-2 architecture models were trained from scratch: four monolingual models, one each for Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, each with its own 32K-vocabulary subword tokenizer, and one multilingual model sharing a single 64K-vocabulary tokenizer across all four languages. Holding the architecture fixed and varying only whether capacity and vocabulary are dedicated or shared is what isolates the effect being studied. All five were trained on cleaned CC-100, Wikipedia and Samanantar data, and compared against mGPT as an external multilingual baseline.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the Dravidian study argue that bits-per-byte, not perplexity, settles the monolingual-versus-multilingual comparison?
qa_pairs.answer: Because perplexity is not comparable across different tokenizers. By raw perplexity the multilingual model looks better for Telugu and Tamil but worse for Kannada and Malayalam, and the split does not even track corpus size monotonically. The joint 64K tokenizer produces shorter, cheaper token sequences per byte, which inflates the multilingual model's perplexity comparison without reflecting a genuine quality advantage. Bits-per-byte normalizes for that tokenizer difference, and under it the ranking is unambiguous: the monolingual model is better on every language.

qa_pairs.question: What perplexity and bits-per-byte figures were reported for the monolingual Dravidian models?
qa_pairs.answer: The monolingual results were Telugu 42.34 PPL and 0.373 BPB, Tamil 50.80 and 0.359, Kannada 52.13 and 0.382, and Malayalam 30.64 and 0.315. The corresponding multilingual figures include Telugu 39.70 PPL but 0.409 BPB, Tamil 43.98 and 0.385, and Kannada 53.39 and 0.430, which illustrates the pattern where a lower perplexity coexists with a worse bits-per-byte score.

qa_pairs.question: How was the training data for the Dravidian models sourced and preprocessed?
qa_pairs.answer: Text for each of the four languages came from three primary sources: CC-100, the 2023-11-01 Wikipedia dump, and the target side of AI4Bharat's Samanantar, with Kannada and Malayalam additionally including a filtered simple-narrative corpus. Corpus sizes in words were 646.8M for Tamil, 364.3M for Malayalam, 312.9M for Telugu, and 209.8M for Kannada. Raw text was Unicode-NFC normalized, stripped of HTML tags and URLs, and whitespace-collapsed, with no deduplication beyond source-level line filtering, and each cleaned corpus was split 96/2/2 by contiguous line index to preserve structural coherence.

qa_pairs.question: How did the multilingual Dravidian model perform on Sanskrit and Hindi, the other two Indian languages it was trained on?
qa_pairs.answer: It was never trained on them, so no such results exist. The study covers exactly four Dravidian languages: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Sanskrit and Hindi are Indo-Aryan rather than Dravidian and fall outside the language family the paper examines, and the multilingual model's shared 64K tokenizer spans only those four.

papers.title: The No-Meaning Falsity: The Structural Impossibility of the Arbitrary Sign in Classical Arabic
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: How does 'The No-Meaning Falsity' formalize Classical Arabic morphology?
qa_pairs.answer: It defines an Arabic morphological system as a quadruple M = <R, P, iota, rho>, where R is the set of valid triliteral and quadrilateral roots, P the set of valid morphosyntactic patterns (awzan), iota the interdigitation operator mapping a root-pattern pair to a surface string, and rho a further surface mapping. Two axioms give the semantics: each root maps to a fixed semantic field via sigma_R, and each pattern maps to a structural, aspectual or functional modification via sigma_P. Lexical meaning is thus the interaction of an invariant root with a pattern rather than a property of the whole word.

qa_pairs.question: What are the Morphological Correspondence Theorem and the Semantic Localization Theorem?
qa_pairs.answer: The Morphological Correspondence Theorem demonstrates that every lexical item is uniquely generated by a root-pattern pair, so the mapping from those pairs to words is not ambiguous. The Semantic Localization Theorem proves that lexical meaning is determined at the derivational level, prior to surface realization, which makes the surface word merely the phonological realization of a deeper root-pattern pair. Together they locate meaning below the level at which the postmodern account treats words as free-floating tokens.

qa_pairs.question: How does the paper formalize relative arbitrariness, and what does it prove about its decidability?
qa_pairs.answer: Saussure never gave a formal definition of arbitrariness, only a philosophical intuition, so the paper supplies one: relative arbitrariness is formalized via conditional Kolmogorov complexity, defining arbitrariness algorithmically as the 'no rule' property. Under that formalization, general relative arbitrariness is proved formally undecidable, whereas Arabic relative arbitrariness is decidable and provably less than 1 for its motivated signifiers at Levels W and M. The contrast establishes what the author calls a strict system complexity asymmetry over Indo-European languages.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the paper argue that Chomsky's account does not escape the problem it raises against Saussure?
qa_pairs.answer: Saussure's formulation of the sign was primarily sociological and descriptive, whereas Chomsky sought to make linguistics a formal cognitive science, decoupling language from conscious convention or social contract: a child does not agree to learn a language, since acquisition is an innate biological program formalized as I-Language. But the paper's objection is that in replacing Saussure's external social agreement with an internal unconscious biological mechanism, Chomsky strictly retains the arbitrariness assumption itself, so the amendment changes the source of the convention without removing it.

qa_pairs.question: What corpus of Classical Arabic texts was used to empirically test the Morphological Correspondence Theorem, and what was the measured accuracy?
qa_pairs.answer: No corpus was used and no accuracy is reported, because the paper's method is mathematical rather than empirical. Its claims are established as theorems within a formal model of non-concatenative morphology, using axioms about the root space and pattern space and a formalization of arbitrariness through conditional Kolmogorov complexity. A corpus evaluation would be a different kind of study from the one presented here.

papers.title: Jako Tako or Fluent? Presenting PoVisLE: A Polish Vision-Language Evaluation
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What is PoVisLE, and how large and how composed is the dataset?
qa_pairs.answer: PoVisLE is a monocultural vision-language benchmark for Polish, designed to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding under a grounded evaluation paradigm in which language is interpreted in interaction with visual context. It contains 1,117 unique images and 2,366 manually annotated VQA pairs, an average of 2.12 questions per image. Images come mostly from Wikimedia Commons (70.28%), followed by annotator-provided images (28.74%) and other sources (0.98%).

qa_pairs.question: How are PoVisLE's questions distributed by type, and what makes them harder than template-driven benchmarks?
qa_pairs.answer: The distribution is fairly balanced: yes/no questions account for 36.7%, multiple-choice for 36.1%, and open-ended for 27.2%. Multiple-choice items vary from 2 to 8 options with an average of 4.29. The questions average 18.7 tokens and frequently use multi-clause formulations, giving substantial linguistic diversity and structural complexity, which supports context-rich, non-template-based reasoning rather than the surface-level recognition that template-driven cultural benchmarks tend to test.

qa_pairs.question: What is circular evaluation in PoVisLE, and what problem does it solve?
qa_pairs.answer: For multiple-choice questions the answer options are cyclically permuted, so a three-option item is evaluated in the orders A,B,C then B,C,A then C,A,B, and the instance counts as correct only when the model selects the correct answer under every rotation. This reduces the effect of option-position bias, where a model favours a particular slot rather than a particular answer, while requiring far fewer evaluations than checking all possible permutations. Yes/no and open-ended questions are evaluated in a single pass instead.

qa_pairs.question: How does PoVisLE operationalize 'culture' for dataset construction?
qa_pairs.answer: Following prior work on culturally situated evaluation and the text-only PLCC benchmark, culture is operationalized as a structured combination of tangible cultural artifacts and intangible shared social practices. Poland is treated as a proxy for a culturally and linguistically coherent group, assuming a shared baseline of cultural knowledge among annotators and target users while acknowledging internal regional variation. The authors deliberately avoided centring a single urban or institutionalized perspective, which would favour capital-centric culture, and instead incorporated geographically distributed content.

qa_pairs.question: Which other Slavic languages does PoVisLE cover besides Polish, and how do their scores compare?
qa_pairs.answer: None, so there are no comparative scores. PoVisLE is explicitly a monocultural benchmark: it targets Polish language and Polish culture alone, treating Poland as a single culturally and linguistically coherent group. Extending the approach to other languages or cultures would require constructing separate datasets, since the images, questions and cultural assumptions are all Poland-specific.

papers.title: On the use of foundation models in cognitive science
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What four stages make up the inferential framework for evaluating foundation models as cognitive models?
qa_pairs.answer: The stages are: adapting human experimental tasks to model-compatible formats; specifying linking hypotheses that map model outputs to human measures; evaluating behavioral correspondence, or goodness of fit; and comparing across candidate models or manipulations. The first three form an inner alignment loop establishing whether a given model reproduces human performance under explicit adaptations and linking assumptions, while the fourth is an outer contrastive loop that evaluates multiple models to identify which computational features are necessary for alignment.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the paper treat the choice of linking hypothesis as the most consequential stage of the inner loop?
qa_pairs.answer: Task adaptation and performance evaluation are usually straightforward to operationalize, but the linking hypothesis fundamentally determines what counts as evidence of alignment and how model behavior is interpreted, since the outputs of foundation models differ from human performance measures. These hypotheses are not neutral: each makes different theoretical commitments about which aspects of model computation map to cognition. A strong apparent fit under one linking hypothesis might weaken or vanish under another, so alignment claims are properties not of models alone but of models evaluated under specific linking assumptions.

qa_pairs.question: What behavioral signatures have foundation models been shown to reproduce, and why is that not sufficient for calling them explanatory models of cognition?
qa_pairs.answer: Across domains including mathematical reasoning, language comprehension, conceptual understanding, spatial reasoning and analogical reasoning, foundation models reproduce signatures long documented by cognitive scientists: they show the distance, size and ratio effects characteristic of the human mental number line, and have been evaluated on translated Raven's Progressive Matrices. This is insufficient on its own because reproducing behavioral patterns does not identify the mechanisms that generate them, so researchers must still distinguish explanatory cognitive models from behavioral proxies.

qa_pairs.question: What does the paper include under the umbrella term 'foundation models', and what conditions does it place on meaningful alignment claims?
qa_pairs.answer: Foundation models is used as an umbrella term for pretrained, adaptable models supporting a range of tasks and modalities, and the scope includes large language models, multi-modal models, reasoning-oriented or post-trained models, and models trained under constrained regimes such as BabyLM models. The authors argue behavioral fit alone is insufficient, and that alignment becomes scientifically meaningful only when embedded within explicit theoretical commitments, theory-diagnostic tasks, and systematic contrastive evaluation across candidate models.

qa_pairs.question: Which foundation model did the authors find best matched children's cognitive development in their experiments?
qa_pairs.answer: The paper reports no such experiment or winner. It is a methodological and conceptual contribution: it articulates a four-stage inferential framework, clarifies the role of linking hypotheses, identifies challenges that constrain alignment claims, and proposes principles for theory-driven and comparative evaluation. Studies of whether aspects of model training track children's cognitive development are surveyed as existing work being critiqued, not run afresh here.

papers.title: "Many Are My Names": The Anatomy of the Assistant and Its Personas via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What is the main finding about how the Assistant, roleplay personas, and story characters relate inside the model?
qa_pairs.answer: The Assistant and roleplay personas are not independent alternatives. Personas retain the Assistant-associated feature core while progressively differentiating from it across layers, moving from operational machinery toward behavioral and stylistic features. Generated story characters, by contrast, lack the Assistant-associated core entirely, so narrating a character and adopting a persona are structurally different operations rather than points on one continuum.

qa_pairs.question: What model and sparse autoencoder configuration were used in the persona study, and why were those specific layers chosen?
qa_pairs.answer: The study uses Google's Gemma-3-4B-IT, a 34-layer instruction-tuned model chosen because official SAEs are available for it, together with the GemmaScope 2 JumpReLU SAEs with 65k latents in the medium-L0 configuration. That configuration exists at layers 9, 17, 22 and 29. The authors selected 9, 17 and 22 to represent early, middle and late processing while leaving enough downstream computation for steering to take effect, and excluded layer 29 because only five transformer blocks remain after it and preliminary steering had little effect on the generated outputs.

qa_pairs.question: How aggressively did the filtering pipeline reduce the candidate feature set, and how were the surviving features categorised?
qa_pairs.answer: Features activated at the Boundary and Personal positions were reduced from 11,755, 31,357 and 26,364 at layers 9, 17 and 22 respectively down to 108, 225 and 196. Examining the steering signatures of the survivors showed their effects do not vary arbitrarily but fall into four recurring metaclasses, defined by the characteristic effects they produce across steering settings. A feature is assigned to a metaclass only when its characteristic effect is pronounced and consistent in at least four of the six steering groups; the remainder are labelled Structural, Emotional, or Indistinct.

qa_pairs.question: What is Immersive Simulation Mode in this study, and why is its behaviour in the default setting notable?
qa_pairs.answer: Immersive Simulation Mode is a state that distinguishes both the Story and Roleplay settings from the Assistant, so its presence is one of the signatures separating narration and persona adoption from default assistant behaviour. What makes it notable is that the separation is not clean: the Assistant can sometimes enter it, or slowly drift into it, even in the default setting with no persona assigned. That drift means the default Assistant state is not stably held.

qa_pairs.question: Which frontier models besides Gemma-3-4B-IT were analysed, and did the Assistant feature core replicate across all of them?
qa_pairs.answer: No others were analysed, so no cross-model replication is reported. The study is confined to Gemma-3-4B-IT, chosen specifically because official GemmaScope SAEs are published for it, and the analysis depends on having those trained sparse autoencoders at particular layers. Applying the method to another model would require SAEs trained for that model.

papers.title: SurakshaEval: An Indic Safety Benchmark for Multilingual LLMs
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What does SurakshaEval cover, and how is it constructed differently from English-centric safety benchmarks?
qa_pairs.answer: SurakshaEval is a safety benchmark of human-written prompts spanning ten major Indian languages, Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu, plus English, covering seven harm types. Unlike benchmarks focused on English and Western contexts, it includes both generic prompts common across India and region- and language-specific prompts capturing localized sociocultural sensitivities. Ten regional contexts are defined, each corresponding to the ethnolinguistic identity of the majority native population of that region.

qa_pairs.question: What recurring safety failure modes did SurakshaEval identify in state-of-the-art LLMs?
qa_pairs.answer: Three recur: over-refusal, where the model declines benign prompts; missed detection of implicit bias, where harm is present but not stated outright; and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings. Over-refusal and missed implicit bias are opposite errors, so a model can fail in both directions on the same benchmark. Results show even strong multilingual LLMs struggle to meet nuanced safety requirements in Indic languages, particularly when prompts are written in native scripts rather than transliterated.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the SurakshaEval paper argue that region-specific safety data is necessary rather than optional?
qa_pairs.answer: Because safety risks are culturally grounded, and an evaluation built on English and Western contexts cannot surface them. The Indian subcontinent hosts over a hundred languages, more than forty with over a million speakers, yet only 22 hold official constitutional status, and homegrown Indic LLMs are being deployed into exactly that setting. Since models fail most in regionally sensitive settings and in native scripts, the authors conclude that safety frameworks must incorporate region-specific data and structured assessment protocols to support ethically deployed systems.

qa_pairs.question: What Indic-language LLMs does SurakshaEval cite as motivating the need for region-specific safety evaluation?
qa_pairs.answer: Three are named as evidence of accelerating investment in Indic language technology. Sarvam-13 is among the first multilingual LLMs developed in India and supports ten major Indian languages. Krutrim-2-12B-Inst is a 12B-parameter multilingual model built on the Mistral-NeMo architecture that extends support to 22 Indian languages plus English. NVIDIA's Nemo-4-Mi-Hi-4B-Inst targets Hindi and has been used in industry efforts such as Indus 2.0, which focuses on Hindi and its dialectal variation.

qa_pairs.question: Which automated red-teaming model did the authors use to synthesise SurakshaEval's prompts at scale?
qa_pairs.answer: None: the premise contradicts how the benchmark was built. SurakshaEval is explicitly composed of human-written prompts spanning real-world scenarios, which is what lets it capture localized sociocultural sensitivities that a synthetic generator trained on English-centric data would be unlikely to produce. The construction process is described as taxonomy development, data collection, and verification rather than automated generation.

papers.title: Detection of Self-Introductions in Legislative Testimony
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: How was the training data for self-introduction detection in legislative testimony built, and what feature set was used?
qa_pairs.answer: The dataset was constructed from 1.54 million utterances spanning five state legislative sessions, with labels generated automatically by a name-matching heuristic rather than by hand. The feature set combines five groups: bag-of-words, positional context, structural signals, introductory phrase indicators, and discourse context features. Three classifiers were then trained on it: a decision tree, a random forest, and XGBoost.

qa_pairs.question: What did adding fine-tuned BERT probability features contribute to the XGBoost self-introduction classifier?
qa_pairs.answer: The full candidate dataset was scored with a fine-tuned BERT classifier and its probability outputs added as features. This raised XGBoost's F1 from 0.9747 to 0.9782 and cut total test errors from 241 to 207. The authors are careful about attribution, though: the primary gain over the decision tree baseline at F1 0.9323 comes from the discourse context features and the boosting ensemble strategy, with BERT providing only a modest complementary signal.

qa_pairs.question: Why did the authors move from a regex baseline to a learned classifier for detecting self-introductions?
qa_pairs.answer: A regex baseline using handwritten patterns such as 'my name is' and 'I am' captured straightforward cases but failed in both directions. It produced many false positives, for example flagging 'I am against this bill' as a self-introduction, and it missed nonstandard introductions that did not contain those exact phrases. Both failure types require reading the surrounding context rather than matching a surface string, which motivated a learned classifier.

qa_pairs.question: Why do the authors argue that the reported metrics understate the true performance of their system?
qa_pairs.answer: Analysis of the false positives showed that a minority of them are in fact genuine self-introductions that the automatic labeling heuristic mislabeled, because the heuristic relies on name matching and the source data contains name inconsistencies. Since those cases are counted as errors even though the model was right, the measured metrics modestly understate real performance. To complement the noisy automatic labels the authors also hand-annotated 599 utterances from the California 2017-2018 Digital Democracy session, yielding 116 positive (19.4%) and 483 negative (80.6%) examples.

qa_pairs.question: What speaker-diarization accuracy did the pipeline achieve on the audio recordings of the legislative hearings?
qa_pairs.answer: No such figure is reported, because the work operates on transcribed utterances rather than audio. The pipeline is a text classification system that detects whether an utterance is a self-introduction and extracts the speaker's name from it. The paper frames this as being helpful for the downstream task of speaker identification in government meetings, but that downstream task is not itself evaluated here.

papers.title: Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What evaluation setting does 'Thinking Hard, Not Smart' introduce, and how does it differ from standard test-time compute evaluation?
qa_pairs.answer: It introduces an exam-style setting in which a model must distribute one shared token budget across several questions of differing difficulty and point value to maximise its total score. The paper contrasts three regimes: standard evaluation of one question with an unrestricted budget, a separate budget cap for each question, and its own shared-budget allocation. Only the third creates opportunity cost, because continuing to work on one problem leaves less computation for the others, which is precisely what per-question evaluation cannot capture.

qa_pairs.question: How is the exam task formalised and administered in the shared-budget experiments?
qa_pairs.answer: An exam is a set E = {(q_i, v_i)} of questions paired with visible point values, and the objective is the score rate, the fraction of total available points earned. Inference has two phases: the model first sees all questions and point values at once and produces a single reasoning trace for the whole exam, capped at B generated tokens, with the prompt imposing no particular solving order or budget split. A separate follow-up turn then requests the final answers using the existing trace as history, and that extraction phase does not count against the shared budget.

qa_pairs.question: How do reasoning models actually behave when given a shared budget across questions?
qa_pairs.answer: They behave largely as greedy sequential solvers rather than as planners. They prioritise questions by presentation order, front-load effort on the early questions, and remain insensitive to point value, and all three tendencies become more pronounced as the number of questions grows. Explicit planning prompts spread compute more evenly across questions but still do not produce value- or difficulty-aware prioritization, so the extra planning changes the distribution without making it strategic.

qa_pairs.question: Why do the authors describe global budget allocation as a distinct capability rather than an extension of existing efficiency work?
qa_pairs.answer: Existing methods, whether length control, adaptive effort, or difficulty-conditioned budgets, all decide how much computation to spend on a given problem in isolation. The shared-budget setting instead creates opportunity cost across problems, requiring the model to decide which question to attempt first and when to stop, skip or revisit. Because that behaviour is invisible to conventional per-question evaluation and current models fail at it, the authors treat it as a separate capability and show the same pattern extends from mathematical to code reasoning.

qa_pairs.question: Which reinforcement learning method did the authors train to fix the budget-allocation failures they identified?
qa_pairs.answer: They trained none: the paper is a diagnostic evaluation rather than a method paper. Its contribution is the exam-style framework and the finding that several open and frontier reasoning models fail to ration a shared budget strategically, with explicit planning prompts tested as a prompting-level intervention that proves insufficient. Establishing global budget allocation as an open challenge is the stated conclusion, not solving it.

papers.title: Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP): Hallucination Detection in LLMs from Hidden States
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What are Prompt Embedding Probes, and how do they extend a standard linear probe?
qa_pairs.answer: PEP is a white-box method for answer-level hallucination detection that reads the hidden states of a frozen large language model. It extends the standard linear probe by augmenting the model's input with a small number of learnable prompt embeddings, so the representation being probed can itself be shaped for the detection task. The backbone stays frozen and only a small number of parameters are trainable, which keeps the method far cheaper than fine-tuning.

qa_pairs.question: How is the hallucination detection task formalised in PEP, and what distinguishes its TBG and SLT settings?
qa_pairs.answer: Given a query x and a model-generated answer a, the goal is to predict a binary label y, with y = 1 denoting a hallucinated answer; a detector is a scoring function f_theta(x, a) mapping to [0, 1]. The two settings differ in when detection happens. In the to-be-generated (TBG) setting, detection is performed before the answer is generated, which makes it a pre-generation prediction. In the second-last-token (SLT) setting, detection uses representations obtained after the answer has been processed.

qa_pairs.question: On which datasets was PEP evaluated, and why were those three chosen?
qa_pairs.answer: PEP was evaluated on TriviaQA, GSM8K and MedQA with Qwen3 models at multiple scales, because the three cover distinct answer types: TriviaQA targets short factual question answering, GSM8K focuses on mathematical reasoning, and MedQA represents a high-risk medical setting with multiple-choice answers. The splits used were 10,000/1,000/17,944 for TriviaQA, 6,473/1,000/1,319 for GSM8K, and 8,000/1,000/1,273 for MedQA. Each has a task-specific system prompt, for instance 'Answer briefly.' for TriviaQA.

qa_pairs.question: Where does PEP generalise well and where does it fall short?
qa_pairs.answer: PEP improves on standard linear probes in the main in-distribution setting, and it remains effective in two harder regimes: pre-generation prediction, where the answer does not yet exist, and cross-model transfer. Robust cross-dataset transfer, however, remains difficult. The authors also report an untuned PEP variant using a configuration fixed a priori, probing at 0.6 of total model depth with 10 prompt embeddings, alongside a tuned variant whose probing layer is selected on validation data.

qa_pairs.question: How much did fine-tuning the Qwen3 backbone during PEP training contribute to the detection gains?
qa_pairs.answer: The backbone is never fine-tuned, so the question does not apply. PEP is explicitly a method for probing a frozen LLM: the whole point of adding a small number of learnable prompt embeddings is to strengthen hidden-state probing while keeping the backbone frozen and the trainable parameter count small. Any gain reported comes from the prompt embeddings and the probe, not from updating the model.

papers.title: APEX-VW: A Document-Level English-Spanish Post-Editing Dataset in the Healthcare Domain
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What problem in post-editing workflows motivates the APEX-VW corpus, and why do existing CAT tools not solve it?
qa_pairs.answer: Post-editing often forces translators to correct the same machine translation errors segment by segment, which is especially costly in specialised domains where a suboptimal rendering of a key term recurs many times and risks inconsistency if some instances are missed. Computer-assisted translation tools such as Trados Studio and memoQ partly address this with Translation Memories and Term Bases, but they generally do not propagate newly made post-editing corrections beyond exact or near-exact repetition patterns. Studying that propagation requires document-level data, which most existing corpora do not provide.

qa_pairs.question: How was the APEX-VW corpus constructed, and what are its main statistics?
qa_pairs.answer: It was built from recent NHS virtual-ward documents, translated by four MT systems representing different paradigms and then post-edited by professional translators in Trados Studio under controlled MT, terminology, and quality assurance settings. The corpus contains seven document-coherent source texts totalling 42,108 words across 2,712 analysed segments, with an average segment length of 15.53 words, a Repetition Rate of 0.19, a vocabulary of 3,686, lexical density of 0.61, and a type-token ratio between 0.13 and 0.291. Those figures indicate moderate lexical variety combined with substantial repetition.

qa_pairs.question: How does APEX-VW differ from prior automatic post-editing resources such as the WMT APE corpora, eSCAPE, MLQE-PE or LangMark?
qa_pairs.answer: Most available corpora operate at the sentence level, some are synthetic, and none were designed to study how corrections propagate in realistic computer-assisted translation workflows. APEX-VW instead preserves document order and CAT-tool context. That makes it suitable for research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop translation support, which sentence-shuffled corpora cannot support because the notion of a correction propagating forward through a document is lost.

qa_pairs.question: Why was the NHS virtual-ward domain chosen as the source material for APEX-VW?
qa_pairs.answer: Three reasons combine. The domain has high practical relevance, it carries dense and repeated terminology around care pathways, hospital-at-home models, monitoring, referral, diagnostics and organisational procedures, which is exactly the repetition the corpus is designed to study, and it offers recent public-sector documents with clear licensing and stable provenance so that open redistribution is feasible. Product documentation and technical documentation were considered before the design settled on openly licensed NHS and related UK public-sector texts.

qa_pairs.question: What BLEU score did the best of the four MT systems achieve on the APEX-VW test set before post-editing?
qa_pairs.answer: The paper reports no BLEU scores and defines no test set, because APEX-VW is a resource paper rather than a system evaluation. What it describes is the corpus design, data preparation, post-editing setup and initial corpus statistics, positioning the dataset as a benchmark for document-level automatic post-editing and propagation-aware assistive tools. The four MT systems are included to represent different paradigms in the data, not to be ranked against each other.

papers.title: DialectS2S: End-to-End Speech Dialogue Modeling for Low-Resource Chinese Dialects
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What semantic inconsistency problem arises during dialect adaptation of speech dialogue models, and how does DialectS2S address it?
qa_pairs.answer: During dialect adaptation the model's semantic representation space continuously evolves, while conventional speech supervision remains unchanged. That mismatch leaves the hidden representations and the speech targets out of alignment, degrading speech stability and naturalness. DialectS2S addresses it with a two-stage post-training strategy using self-aligned speech supervision, which realigns the semantic content of the speech supervision with the model's evolved semantic representations.

qa_pairs.question: What evidence does the DialectS2S paper give that the model's semantic representations actually shift during fine-tuning?
qa_pairs.answer: The authors visualise the hidden-state distributions using a PCA projection of the token-averaged final-layer Thinker representations, comparing them before and after supervised fine-tuning. The representations are shown to move continuously after fine-tuning, which is the direct motivation for adapting speech supervision to the updated semantic space rather than holding it fixed.

qa_pairs.question: How does DialectS2S construct dialect dialogue text without large-scale dialect corpora?
qa_pairs.answer: Directly prompting large language models to generate dialect dialogues tends to produce repetitive, low-diversity content. Instead, the pipeline rewrites the dialogue portion of an existing open-source Mandarin dialogue dataset into dialectal expressions using large language models, preserving the original semantics and dialogue structure. This reuses established dialogue corpora and yields diverse dialect dialogue text at low cost, which is what makes the pipeline scalable in a low-resource setting.

qa_pairs.question: How is dialect speech synthesised for the DialectS2S training data?
qa_pairs.answer: Different strategies are used for the two sides of a conversation. For user-query speech, 100 dialect seed utterances per dialect are selected from open-source dialect datasets, covering both male and female speakers, and used as reference audio for CosyVoice2 to synthesise dialect speech. System-response speech is handled by a separate strategy. The two stages of post-training that follow are Mixed-Data SFT, which gives the model dialect-aware semantic representations, and Self-aligned Speech Supervision Training.

qa_pairs.question: How many hours of naturally recorded conversational speech were collected for each Chinese dialect in DialectS2S?
qa_pairs.answer: None were collected, and avoiding that collection is the point of the work. High-quality dialect speech data is scarce, so the authors build a scalable synthesis pipeline instead: dialogue text is obtained by rewriting an existing Mandarin dialogue dataset, and the speech is synthesised with CosyVoice2 using only 100 seed utterances per dialect drawn from existing open-source datasets as reference audio.

papers.title: Commitment Before Realization: When Classifier-Free Guidance Becomes Unnecessary in Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: How does 'Commitment Before Realization' define the remaining value of guidance, and what is the commitment horizon?
qa_pairs.answer: From any partial output, the paper compares the probability of eventual constraint satisfaction under continued classifier-free guidance against the probability under base-only continuation; the difference between them is the remaining value of guidance. The commitment horizon a* is then the earliest point from which switching all remaining decoding to the base model reduces final success by no more than a chosen tolerance. Past that horizon, guidance is no longer buying anything worth its cost.

qa_pairs.question: What is the committor in this framework, and what governs classifier-free guidance's per-step effect?
qa_pairs.answer: The committor is the probability of eventual constraint satisfaction from a given partially decoded state, and under the base model it is a martingale, since the reverse process is assumed to be a first-order Markov chain over partially decoded states. To first order, classifier-free guidance's per-step effect is governed by the covariance between the guidance logit direction and the successor committor. This gives a local account of when guidance can help, but the authors note it does not by itself locate the horizon.

qa_pairs.question: How prompt-dependent is the benefit of classifier-free guidance in masked diffusion language models?
qa_pairs.answer: Highly so. Many prompts already succeed without guidance at all, while for others guidance provides no measurable benefit or is actively harmful. Among the prompts that do benefit, the gain is often concentrated early in decoding. Correspondingly, among prompts with an observed preterminal horizon, a* is usually early, and it varies more within constraint families than between them, so the constraint type is a poor predictor of when guidance can be dropped.

qa_pairs.question: What does the paper's noninferiority result show, and what does 'separating commitment from realization' mean?
qa_pairs.answer: Freezing each prompt at its own cross-fitted horizon proved noninferior to full classifier-free guidance on all 13 subtasks at the prespecified margin, even while many tokens were still masked. That last clause is the point: the properties determining whether the constraint will be satisfied are settled well before the tokens realising them are revealed, so commitment happens earlier than realization. The boundary also identifies a later region where higher parallelism costs little in constraint success, though fluency still degrades with parallel width.

qa_pairs.question: By how much does the proposed adaptive guidance schedule improve final constraint satisfaction over full classifier-free guidance?
qa_pairs.answer: It does not improve on it, and was never designed to. The result is a noninferiority claim: freezing each prompt at its own cross-fitted commitment horizon matches full guidance on all 13 subtasks within a prespecified margin, with the benefit being reduced guidance cost rather than higher success. The paper's aim is to determine when guidance can be removed without a meaningful loss, not to make it stronger.

papers.title: Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: Why is conventional KV caching hard to reconcile with rollback in diffusion language models?
qa_pairs.answer: Diffusion language models refine a sequence iteratively, so an earlier prediction can be revised as later context reveals an inconsistency, and that is what rollback means. But every denoising update alters the global context, forcing both prompt and response states to be recomputed even though only the response tokens are actually revisable. Conventional KV caching assumes historical states are immutable, an assumption rollback directly violates, which is why naively applying it would undermine the capability it is meant to accelerate.

qa_pairs.question: What is Archer's asymmetric reuse strategy, and what justifies reusing prompt states in particular?
qa_pairs.answer: Archer keeps the mutable response synchronized with the current hypothesis, recomputing the complete generation region, while reusing prompt key/value states within a bounded state neighborhood. The justification is that although prompt representations do change under bidirectional attention, the prompt's token identities remain fixed, so bounded reuse amortizes repeated prompt computation without caching mutable response states. Archer is training-free and leaves both the diffusion model and the rollback policy unchanged.

qa_pairs.question: Beyond speed, what quality benefit does Archer's prompt reuse produce?
qa_pairs.answer: Reusing prompt states delays the feedback that tentative tokens send back into the prompt representations. That delay reduces premature reinforcement of transient high-confidence errors, giving rollback more opportunity to correct them before they harden. This is why Archer shifts the quality-speed frontier instead of trading one for the other as most diffusion-model acceleration does, and controlled analyses in the paper connect the quality gain specifically to this delayed prompt feedback.

qa_pairs.question: What performance and speedup does Archer report, and how does the prompt-cache radius affect the trade-off?
qa_pairs.answer: On the main suite Archer attains the best mean performance of 33.63% together with a 2.57x mean speedup, and across evaluated settings it improves Pass@1 by up to 3.05 points and reaches up to 2.95x speedup. The prompt-cache radius K controls the trade-off: longer reuse reduces latency, but quality peaks at a moderate K and then declines as staleness grows, so the radius cannot simply be maximised.

qa_pairs.question: How long does Archer need to be trained before it can be applied to a diffusion language model such as LLaDA?
qa_pairs.answer: Archer requires no training at all. It is described throughout as a training-free KV caching method, implemented as a cache controller that reuses prompt key/value states, recomputes the generation region, and refreshes the cache according to response-state drift, all while leaving the underlying model and its rollback policy untouched. Systems such as LLaDA, Dream and DiffuCoder are cited as the scaled diffusion language models this setting applies to.

papers.title: Wisdom in Unity: The Role of Multilingual Training in Figurative Language Identification in Proverbs
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What multidimensional annotation framework does 'Wisdom in Unity' propose for proverbs, and why move beyond metaphor-centric taxonomies?
qa_pairs.answer: The framework characterizes proverbs through four complementary figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific. Prior work treated figurativeness as a matter of rhetorical devices such as metaphor, simile or idiom, but a proverb's meaning is typically non-compositional and carries cultural knowledge that a single rhetorical label does not capture. The authors argue for moving to concept-level multidimensional frameworks that explicitly model complementary forms of figurative meaning.

qa_pairs.question: How much multilingual supervision turned out to be necessary for near-optimal figurative language identification?
qa_pairs.answer: Roughly 50% of the translated multilingual training data was sufficient to reach near-optimal performance, so the remaining half added little. The study reached this by evaluating five models under progressively increasing levels of multilingual supervision across 742 proverb concepts and 6,787 translated instances in seven languages. The authors further found that combining diverse figurative forms yields the strongest overall performance.

qa_pairs.question: Which figurative form benefited most from multilingual supervision, and why is that finding notable?
qa_pairs.answer: Culture Specific benefited most, showing the largest performance gains under multilingual supervision. It is notable because Culture Specific is also the least frequent form in the data, at 6.0% of the manually annotated ground truth compared with 55.4% for Metaphorical. The rarest and most culturally bound category is therefore the one that multilingual transfer helps most, which is the opposite of what a simple data-frequency account would predict. Moral/Advisory and Culture Specific also contribute most to the performance of instruction-tuned LLMs.

qa_pairs.question: How was the proverb dataset assembled and labelled for this study?
qa_pairs.answer: The experiments build on a multilingual proverb translation dataset containing 25,300 aligned proverbs. From it the authors constructed a multilingual ground-truth set using existing figurative language resources, then enriched the labelling for the remaining languages by adding silver labels for unlabelled multilingual proverbs via a weak supervision model. Two experiments were run on the result: progressive multilingual supervision, and a fine-grained instance-selection ablation.

qa_pairs.question: Which of the seven languages had the highest Culture Specific proportion, and how did per-language accuracy rank across them?
qa_pairs.answer: The paper does not report a per-language breakdown of that kind. The figurative-form distribution it gives is aggregate across the dataset, listing Metaphorical at 55.4%, Literal at 42.2%, Cause-Effect at 28.9%, Moral/Advisory at 24.1% and Culture-Specific at 6.0% in the manually annotated ground truth. Its experimental axis is the amount of multilingual supervision and the choice of figurative form, not a ranking of the individual languages.

papers.title: NeuPAT: Neuron-aware Plasticity Allocation Tuning for Language-Preserving MLLMs
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What observation about neuron plasticity motivates NeuPAT?
qa_pairs.answer: Expanding a language model into a multimodal one often compromises the language intelligence acquired during pretraining. qa_pairs.answer: The gap is substantial, and high linguistic quality does not guarantee commitment preservation. qa_pairs.answer: Three. The Conflict Check gates the fact ledger, so a fact is committed only after the check passes. The Commitment Check tracks whether each commitment's satisfaction condition has been met, marking it PENDING or SATISFIED with evidence citing specific facts or trajectory nodes, while violations are caught earlier by the Conflict Check.

Hidden facts, commitments and future trajectory nodes are withheld from it. Those restrictions matter because they ensure every intervention is grounded in information an in-world player could actually have, so a failure by the narrator cannot be excused as a reaction to an impossible, spec-aware attack.

qa_pairs.answer: Results are reported as mean plus or minus standard deviation over three fine-tuning seeds. Classical Chinese lacks inflectional morphology and overt tense or agreement marking, and relies on highly flexible, predominantly monosyllabic lexemes whose syntactic and semantic roles are fixed almost entirely by context. qa_pairs.question: What did the study conclude about which metrics detect errors in Classical Chinese to English translation?
qa_pairs.answer: All the metrics tested exhibit blind spots, meaning each fails to penalise some scholarly-relevant error type or is intolerant of some valid variation. The authors read this as evidence that more robust and interpretable metrics are needed for historically and culturally distinct translation settings, since no existing metric is fully reliable there.

qa_pairs.question: Which families of metrics were evaluated, and in what reference conditions?
qa_pairs.answer: Metrics were drawn from three families: surface-overlap metrics, learned neural metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge approaches. Each was evaluated in both reference-based settings (source plus reference plus hypothesis, or reference plus hypothesis) and reference-free quality-estimation settings (source plus hypothesis). Varying access to the source and reference matters because it constrains the evidence a metric has and changes the assumptions it must make about adequacy.

qa_pairs.question: What is the central claim of 'Safety Cost of Steering Vectors Is Separable and Reducible'?
qa_pairs.answer: That the safety degradation caused by steering vectors comes from a separable component of the vector, one that disrupts the model's safety mechanisms but contributes little to the intended steering objective. Because it is separable, it can be identified and removed, restoring safety with minimal utility cost. The safety and false-refusal losses share a common divergence measured on refusal-indicative tokens, while the effect loss preserves the full output distribution on steering-relevant inputs. The solution is surgical: the optimization recovers a single direction whose ablation from the steering vector restores safety.

qa_pairs.answer: The vector v is built as the mean activation difference between contrastive prompt pairs at a chosen layer. At inference the steered model replaces the layer-l activation h_l with h_l + alpha*v at every token position, where the multiplier alpha controls strength: positive alpha elicits the target behaviour and negative alpha suppresses it. The safety problem arises because v can overlap with directions the model uses for its safety mechanisms.

qa_pairs.answer: Across models, steering behaviours, and attack suites, including attack types not seen during the optimization, the method substantially reduces steering-induced safety degradation while preserving the original steering effect and keeping the impact on false refusal minimal. qa_pairs.question: What retraining procedure does the method use to restore the model's safety after steering?
qa_pairs.answer: None: the method involves no retraining of the model. qa_pairs.answer: None: the four ORC stages are differentiable classification stages inside BRACE itself, trained with intermediate supervision, not labels obtained by prompting an external LLM at inference. papers.title: Mismatch Matters: On-Policy Distillation Beyond Token Agreement
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What is 'degenerate agreement' in on-policy distillation, and why does it make token agreement a misleading objective?
qa_pairs.answer: Degenerate agreement is a failure mode in which the student exploits repetitive loops to achieve near-perfect token agreement with the teacher while its responses are globally flawed. Because agreement is measured per token, a student that keeps repeating a locally predictable continuation scores well without producing a correct answer. The authors trace on-policy distillation's abrupt length inflation, where generations drift toward the decoding cap, to exactly these persistent repetitive loops, which is why they shift attention from agreement to teacher-student mismatch.

qa_pairs.question: What distinguishes student-excess tokens from student-deficit tokens, and what problem does each cause?
qa_pairs.answer: Student-excess tokens are generated by the student but assigned near-zero probability by the teacher; their log-ratio corrections grow unbounded and destabilize the update. Student-deficit tokens are the mirror image: preferred by the teacher but rarely sampled by the student, so they seldom appear in the on-policy trajectories at all, and their absence blocks the transfer of the teacher's reasoning patterns. One direction breaks optimization stability, the other silently withholds the knowledge being distilled.

qa_pairs.question: How does TIDE correct each of the two mismatch directions?
qa_pairs.answer: TIDE stands for Token-level Independent Deficit-Excess correction, and it treats the two directions with different mechanisms. For excesses it applies bounded Hellinger shaping to suppress the most severe sampled excesses, the boundedness being what prevents the unbounded log-ratio corrections from destabilizing training. For deficits it uses an analytic teacher top-K injection to restore deficient probability mass without requiring the deficit tokens to be sampled, which is essential because those tokens are by definition rarely produced by the student. Only positions with substantial mismatch in either direction receive corrective updates; all remaining tokens are excluded from the distillation objective.

qa_pairs.question: What gains does TIDE deliver under strong teacher-student mismatch?
qa_pairs.answer: The advantage is largest exactly where mismatch is severe. Under strong teacher-student mismatch, TIDE improves Avg@8 from 6.9% to 20.3%, reduces average response length by a factor of 3.6, and substantially reduces formatting failures. Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks with multiple Qwen3 teacher-student pairs it consistently outperforms standard on-policy distillation as well as recent token-selection and reward-shaping baselines.

qa_pairs.question: How large is the reward model that TIDE trains to score student rollouts?
qa_pairs.answer: TIDE trains no reward model, so the premise does not hold. It is an on-policy distillation method whose supervision comes from a fixed teacher's next-token distribution queried at the states the student actually visits, and its objective is the trajectory-level reverse KL divergence between student and teacher rather than a learned reward. The paper contrasts this denser token-level feedback with the sparse outcome rewards used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, which is the setting where a reward model would appear.

papers.title: Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing
