qa_pairs.answer: The main paired case study produces CantRomZJ1 for Cantonese and MandRomZJ1 for Mandarin, both following the design framework, and schemes for Meixian Hakka, Shanghai Wu, and Nanjing Jianghuai Mandarin are also developed. To make them practical, the authors build open-source infrastructure for structured romanization storage, conversion, parsing, dictionary construction, and input-method generation, plus a community-driven open-source workflow.

qa_pairs.question: How was the design framework evaluated, and what were the results?
qa_pairs.answer: Through speech-to-romanization experiments based on fine-tuning Meta's Massively Multilingual Speech model. Compared with a Pinyin plus Jyutping baseline, the MandRomZJ1 plus CantRomZJ1 condition reduced Cantonese word error rate by 7.80% and character error rate by 10.61%, which the authors take as evidence that cross-lingual romanization alignment improves transfer in low-resource Sinitic speech technology.

qa_pairs.question: Why does CantRomZJ1 preserve the Jyutping initial system rather than reshaping it toward Mandarin symbols?
qa_pairs.answer: Because the Jyutping initials already align well with MandRomZJ1: the stop initials give the unaspirated-aspirated contrast as b:p, d:t, g:k, and the alveolar sibilants map to s, z, c, consistent with MandRomZJ1 and with both correspondence principles. Jyutping <j> for /j/ is also kept rather than changed to <y>, partly because /j/ is analysed as an initial and partly because using <y> would collide with the <yu> already used for /y/, producing forms like <yyu>.

qa_pairs.question: Which large language model did the authors fine-tune on parallel Mandarin-Cantonese text to generate the romanization schemes?
qa_pairs.answer: The romanization schemes are designed by hand from linguistic principles, not generated by a fine-tuned language model. The only model fine-tuning in the paper is of Meta's Massively Multilingual Speech model for the speech-to-romanization evaluation, which tests the schemes rather than creating them.

papers.title: Toward Cultural Alignment: Human-Centered Evaluation of Multimodal AI Stories Across Five African Communities
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What does this study mean by 'cultural alignment', and how did it evaluate it?
qa_pairs.answer: Cultural alignment is community-recognized fit between generated content and lived experience: whether AI-generated multimodal stories reflect the practices, relationships, language, values, and visual expectations of the communities they portray. The evaluation was a community-grounded mixed-methods study with 19 culture representatives across five African communities, combining quantitative annotations with qualitative focus-group discussions.

qa_pairs.question: What was the study's central finding about what cultural alignment depends on?
qa_pairs.answer: That alignment does not depend simply on the presence of recognizable cultural markers, but on how those markers fit the social, linguistic, procedural, and visual context. From the evaluations the authors build a taxonomy comprising five broader cultural marker categories and eight recurring mechanisms of misalignment, so a story can name the right things and still be misaligned if they are used in the wrong way.

qa_pairs.question: What did the study find when it tested multimodal LLM judges as stand-ins for community evaluation?
qa_pairs.answer: Five multimodal LLM judges were evaluated, and their reliability and score calibration varied substantially across the five communities, with no single judge performing consistently across all settings. This motivates community-calibrated evaluation pipelines, where automated judges are validated against community judgments to establish where they can be trusted and where human review is still required.

qa_pairs.question: How were the culturally situated personas for story generation created?
qa_pairs.answer: Using GPT-4.1, through a cascading pipeline of 19 sequential LLM calls in which each attribute is conditioned on the previously generated ones, for example country then community then province then religion then name then gender then age. This dependency-aware process was designed to keep the demographic, cultural, and regional attributes consistent, and the resulting personas were manually reviewed for plausibility.

qa_pairs.question: Which multimodal LLM judge did the study find reliable enough to replace community evaluators across all five African communities?
qa_pairs.answer: None: the study explicitly reports that judge reliability and calibration vary substantially across communities and that no single judge performs consistently across all five. Its recommendation is community-calibrated pipelines in which automated judges are validated against community judgments, not that any judge can replace human review wholesale.

papers.title: Attribute-Based Activation Steering of LLMs for Group-Specific Explanation Generation
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What problem does 'Attribute-Based Activation Steering for Group-Specific Explanation Generation' set out to solve?
qa_pairs.answer: Explanations are only understood well when tailored to the background and abilities of the person being explained to, but prompting alone has been shown insufficient for producing such group-tailored explanations, and other computational methods are missing. The paper investigates whether an LLM can be steered to generate explanations tailored to a specific target group, such as game developers or philosophers.

qa_pairs.question: What are the three main steps of the proposed approach?
qa_pairs.answer: First, extract group-specific attributes of explanatory style and knowledge from explanatory texts written by members of the target group. Second, create attribute-specific activation vectors for each attribute. Third, compute attribute-based steering vectors from those and add them to the LLM's internal activations during inference, enabling fine-grained steering toward the group's style and knowledge.

qa_pairs.question: How were group-specific attributes obtained, and what data source was used?
qa_pairs.answer: The approach only needs texts written by members of specific groups. The authors use Stack Exchange, a set of domain-specific Q&A forums, making the simplifying assumption that answers in a given domain's forum, such as game development, are written by members of that group. A two-stage prompting process then identifies the most important style and knowledge attributes for each of 11 target groups, using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for prompting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for attribute filtering, and Qwen3-Embedding-8B for attribute vector representations.

qa_pairs.question: How was the steering approach evaluated, and how did it compare with prompting and prior steering baselines?
qa_pairs.answer: It was assessed on the specificity and factuality of the generated explanations, plus a study with human experts drawn from the different target groups. Compared with prompting and state-of-the-art steering baselines, the attribute-based approach tailored explanations to the target group significantly better while largely maintaining factuality.

qa_pairs.question: Which LLM did the authors fine-tune on Stack Exchange answers so it would produce group-specific explanations?
qa_pairs.answer: None: the method is activation steering at inference time, not fine-tuning. Stack Exchange texts are used only to extract each group's style and knowledge attributes, which are turned into steering vectors added to a frozen model's activations. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, its 72B variant, and Qwen3-Embedding-8B are used for prompting, filtering, and embedding, not trained.

papers.title: Anchoring Speech with Semantics: A Multimodal Adapter Mechanism for Automatic Speech Recognition in Low-Resource Languages
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: Why is the decoder side a bottleneck for low-resource ASR, and what does SAMA-ASR add to address it?
qa_pairs.answer: Multilingual speech pretraining can transfer shared phonetic representations on the encoder side, but when only a few target-language transcripts exist, the decoder gets little supervised evidence for the target variety's lexical choices, orthographic conventions, common constructions, and meaning-compatible continuations. SAMA-ASR is a lightweight decoder-side adapter that conditions decoding on two anchors: translation-derived semantic embeddings for utterance-level meaning, and a speech embedding to keep decoding grounded when the translations are noisy or incomplete.

qa_pairs.question: How does SAMA-ASR obtain its semantic anchors at inference time?
qa_pairs.answer: Rather than requiring oracle translations, the semantic anchors are generated automatically by an upstream speech-to-text translation model, so deployment does not depend on gold translations. In the paper's implementation Whisper is the ASR backbone and mBERT the semantic text encoder, though the adapter-based anchoring mechanism can in principle attach to other encoder-decoder ASR architectures. Translator-capacity analyses show a compact ST model can still produce useful semantic anchors.

qa_pairs.question: On what data was SAMA-ASR evaluated, and how did it compare with baselines?
qa_pairs.answer: It was evaluated on two 30-hour datasets covering the low-resource Sinitic varieties Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka, each providing paired dialect speech and Mandarin auxiliary translations. SAMA-ASR improved over acoustic-only, prior prompt-based, and semantic-only translation-guided baselines, and remained effective when semantic anchors were produced automatically rather than supplied as oracles.

qa_pairs.question: Why does SAMA-ASR keep an acoustic anchor alongside the semantic anchors instead of relying on translation embeddings alone?
qa_pairs.answer: Because the auxiliary translations can be noisy or incomplete, especially when produced by a compact upstream translator at inference time. The speech embedding keeps the decoder grounded in the actual acoustic evidence so that a bad translation cannot pull the transcription away from what was said; the semantic anchors contribute utterance-level meaning, and the acoustic anchor is the safeguard.

qa_pairs.question: How many hours of Hokkien and Hakka transcripts did the authors add by fine-tuning Whisper's encoder from scratch?
qa_pairs.answer: The paper does not describe adding transcripts or retraining Whisper's encoder from scratch. SAMA-ASR is a lightweight decoder-side adapter trained on the existing 30-hour datasets, and its whole motivation is that target-language transcripts are scarce. The gain comes from conditioning on semantic and acoustic anchors, not from more transcribed data.

papers.title: When Patients Cut In: Extending Clinical Conversational AI Safety to Interruptions
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: Why do interruptions pose a distinct safety problem for clinical voice agents?
qa_pairs.answer: Production clinical voice agents typically use a cascaded speech-to-text then LLM then text-to-speech architecture, and real patients do not wait their turn. When a patient cuts the agent off mid-utterance, clinically required content can be lost even if the model handles cooperative transcripts well. Yet clinical conversational-AI benchmarks almost universally assume the patient waits for the agent to finish, so interruption-induced loss of required content goes unmeasured.

qa_pairs.question: How does this study evaluate interruption recovery?
qa_pairs.answer: It is a transcript-based evaluation that adapts conversation-analytic overlap categories into three operational interruption types, recognitional, competitive, and transitional sub-unit, and tests four deployment-oriented non-reasoning LLM configurations across four cells spanning history-taking (information gathering) and FAQ (information provision). Each response is scored on whether the agent preserves the clinically required content, following a reference-point framing where the failure of interest is an unsafe omission.

qa_pairs.question: What did the results show about how interruptions affect information-gathering versus information-provision tasks?
qa_pairs.answer: In the gathering cells, target-question failure varied across models. In the provision cells, where the arms are directly comparable, failure rose for every model. Rankings differed across cells, and competitive FAQ interruption produced 30 of 30 provision-coverage failures for all four models, with a Wilson 95% interval of 88.6 to 100.0%, against a baseline of 0 of 30 for three models and 4 of 30 for Llama.

qa_pairs.question: What did a brief apology marker such as 'sorry to interrupt' do to recovery, and what does that imply for evaluation?
qa_pairs.answer: Adding the apology marker shifted recovery by tens of percentage points, but inconsistently across models, and for one model it actually reduced recovery. The authors conclude that interruption robustness cannot be reduced to a single score: evaluation must be content-grounded, reported per cell, and matched to the interruption profile of the specific deployment.

qa_pairs.question: Which interruption-robust clinical dialogue model did the authors fine-tune and release?
qa_pairs.answer: None: the paper is an evaluation of four existing deployment-oriented, non-reasoning LLM configurations, not a model-training contribution. Its output is a content-grounded interruption-recovery evaluation method, the three operational interruption types, and per-cell findings, along with accompanying code.

papers.title: Large Language Models Systematically Favor Popular Options: Evidence and Mitigation Across MCQs
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What is 'popularity bias' in multiple-choice evaluation of LLMs, and how is popularity measured?
qa_pairs.answer: Popularity bias is a model's systematic tendency to select popular but incorrect answer options over less popular correct ones. Popularity here means an entity's external familiarity, measured by normalized Wikipedia page views as a model-agnostic proxy. The pattern aligns with confidence miscalibration: the model's confidence stays high even as its accuracy collapses for popular options.

qa_pairs.question: What is PopMCQ, and what did it reveal in its most adversarial setting?
qa_pairs.answer: PopMCQ is a benchmark with six controlled strategies that vary option popularity while holding the question and the correct answer fixed, built from MuSiQue, Natural Questions, EntityQuestions, and WebQuestions. In the most adversarial strategy, where every distractor is more popular than the correct option, models chose popular but wrong answers 66% of the time.

qa_pairs.question: How does PopDebias mitigate popularity bias?
qa_pairs.answer: PopDebias is a lightweight inference-time correction that estimates a popularity prior and removes it from the model's predictions. It requires no fine-tuning, is label-free at test time, using only a small calibration split to fit its parameters, and adds negligible computational cost. Across 22 open-source LLMs from 0.5B to 32B parameters it gave consistent improvements, with accuracy gains up to 54.1 percentage points under strong popularity pressure.

qa_pairs.question: Why does popularity bias particularly distort factual QA benchmarks?
qa_pairs.answer: Because in datasets like EntityQuestions and MuSiQue the correct answers are predominantly low-popularity, with median popularity around 0.09 to 0.10 and more than 49% of gold answers below 0.1. When correct answers are usually the less famous option, a model that leans toward well-known options is systematically pushed toward wrong answers, so uncontrolled distractor popularity confounds the accuracy score.

qa_pairs.question: Which LLM did the authors fine-tune on PopMCQ to remove popularity bias at the weight level?
qa_pairs.answer: None: PopDebias is explicitly a fine-tuning-free, inference-time correction that subtracts an estimated popularity prior, using only a small calibration split. The 22 models from 0.5B to 32B are evaluated as-is with zero-shot max-probability selection, and the mitigation is applied on top of their predictions rather than by retraining them.

papers.title: SHADOWBENCH: Toward Reliable Automatic Evaluation of Semantic Alignment in Autoformalization
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What evaluation failure in autoformalization does SA-Pass address?
qa_pairs.answer: Autoformalization translates informal theorems into proof-assistant code such as Lean, and the hard part of evaluation is judging whether the generated formal statement means the same mathematics as the informal one. Existing metrics can accept type-correct but semantically misaligned statements, or reject correct statements written in a different but equivalent formulation. SA-Pass, Semantic Alignment Pass, is designed to catch both errors.

qa_pairs.question: How does SA-Pass decide whether a generated formal statement gets full credit?
qa_pairs.answer: It tests the statement against auxiliary formal statements called shadows that characterise the intended statement. A generated statement earns full credit only when it compiles, implies each shadow individually (the forward check), and is implied by the conjunction of all shadows (the backward check). A shadow set is complete when the shadows jointly imply the intended statement, so passing both directions means the generated statement is logically equivalent to the intended one.

qa_pairs.question: What is ShadowBench, and how were its checker theorems built?
qa_pairs.answer: ShadowBench is a Lean 4 full-autoformalization benchmark of 178 postgraduate- to research-level problems across eight mathematical areas, equipped with checker theorems for semantic alignment. Checker construction is LLM-assisted and compiler-verified: Qwen3-235B proposes candidate shadow sets and checker theorems, Lean verifies the shadow set is complete, and experts review and guide revisions. It averages about 10 minutes per problem, and for 85% of problems the initial LLM-generated shadow set is already complete.

qa_pairs.question: How well does SA-Pass agree with expert judgment, and how do current systems score on ShadowBench?
qa_pairs.answer: Across outputs from six agentic configurations, SA-Pass reaches 98.8% binary agreement with expert judgments, so it is a reliable automatic proxy. The task itself remains hard: Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with Numina-Lean-Agent reaches a 61.8% compile rate but only 11.2% SA-Pass, meaning most statements that compile are still not semantically aligned.

qa_pairs.question: Which autoformalization model did the authors fine-tune on ShadowBench to raise its SA-Pass score above 50%?
qa_pairs.answer: The paper does not fine-tune an autoformalization model. ShadowBench and SA-Pass are an evaluation contribution: a benchmark with compiler-verified shadow checkers and a metric validated against experts. The reported 11.2% SA-Pass for a strong agentic configuration is presented as evidence that the task is far from solved, not as a number improved by training.

papers.title: Modality Fault Lines: Structural Corruptions Reveal Fragile Omni-Modal Reasoning
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What is a 'modality fault line', and why can clean omni-modal benchmarks miss it?
qa_pairs.answer: A modality fault line is a boundary at which a model's behavior becomes unstable when a modality is still present and human-interpretable but its internal evidence structure has been perturbed. Clean benchmarks, where every channel is present, synchronized, and easy to read, cannot tell whether a model's success depends on stable cross-modal structure or merely on cues that suffice only when inputs are intact.

qa_pairs.question: How does the SCEval protocol differ from missing-modality ablations?
qa_pairs.answer: SCEval keeps the question, answer space, and all modality channels fixed and applies controlled structural corruptions to text, vision, and audio individually and jointly. Crucially every channel remains present and human-interpretable throughout, so the measured accuracy drops reflect structural fragility rather than distribution shift from a removed input. It is built from 273 human-verified tri-modal examples drawn from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR.

qa_pairs.question: What did SCEval find when it evaluated 15 omni-modal systems?
qa_pairs.answer: Structural corruption lowered clean accuracy across the board; text-vision damage formed the most stable shared fault line across models; and multi-modal degradation was non-additive, not a simple function of how many modalities were corrupted. Fragility concentrated in a small set of structural operators, five of the fourteen, and these patterns were largely invariant across model bands.

qa_pairs.question: What conclusion does the paper draw about interpreting clean omni-modal accuracy?
qa_pairs.answer: That a high score on clean text-vision-audio inputs does not establish that a model will stay reliable when cross-modal evidence becomes structurally unreliable. Because clean evaluation cannot distinguish robust cross-modal fusion from reliance on cues sufficient only in intact inputs, structure-corruption diagnostics like SCEval are needed alongside clean benchmarks.

qa_pairs.question: Which omni-modal model did the authors fine-tune on structurally corrupted data to close the fault lines they found?
qa_pairs.answer: None: SCEval is a diagnostic evaluation protocol, and the paper evaluates 15 existing proprietary and open-source systems without training any of them. Its contribution is the modality-fault-line concept, the corruption protocol, and the finding that clean accuracy does not predict structural robustness, not a hardened model.

papers.title: Cloud and On-Premises Deployment of Uzbek Legal RAG via Targeted Retriever Fine-Tuning
papers.generator: claude-sonnet-5 (Claude Code, manual authoring from abstract + section digest)

qa_pairs.question: What two deployment regimes must the Uzbek legal RAG assistant support, and why do they conflict?
qa_pairs.answer: A managed cloud service that maximizes answer quality within a per-token cost ceiling, and an on-premises deployment for clients whose legal data may not leave their infrastructure, which restricts the system to open-weight models on limited local hardware under latency constraints. The two pull in opposite directions: the cloud regime can use strong proprietary models but must watch cost, while the on-premises regime trades model strength for data sovereignty and speed.

qa_pairs.question: What two benchmarks did the authors build for Uzbek legal RAG, and why build evaluation first?
qa_pairs.answer: A retrieval benchmark of 178 expert-annotated legal queries with gold provision spans, and an end-to-end benchmark of 504 expert-curated question-answer pairs scored by an LLM judge. Because no evaluation existed for this setting and the central risk was trusting an unreliable evaluator, they validated the automated judge against human judgments and against an independent-family judge before using it, and report top-5 retrieval accuracy on the retrieval set.

qa_pairs.question: What did the authors conclude about the open-versus-proprietary model gap, and what did they build in response?
qa_pairs.answer: Under both regimes the open-versus-proprietary gap is small and cheaply closed by fine-tuning the retriever. In response they trained UTE-1, which they report as a state-of-the-art open text embedder for Uzbek, and released it along with the benchmarks and evaluation code.

qa_pairs.question: Why do the authors argue against closing the remaining gap by fine-tuning the generator LLM, and what negative result supports this?
qa_pairs.answer: Because it is both impractical and unnecessary: long-context legal Q&A makes generator fine-tuning very hardware-intensive, and legal acts change frequently, so a fine-tuned generator would quickly go stale while a retrieval-based system just re-indexes the updated law. They support this with a reported negative result from a QLoRA experiment, and instead concentrate the fine-tuning effort on the retriever, which is cheaper and more durable.

qa_pairs.question: Which fine-tuned Uzbek generation LLM did the authors release as the core of their production legal assistant?
qa_pairs.answer: They released a fine-tuned embedder, UTE-1, not a fine-tuned generation model. Their explicit finding is that generator fine-tuning for long-context legal Q&A is impractical and unnecessary given how often laws change, backed by a negative QLoRA result; the targeted fine-tuning in the title refers to the retriever.
